title: Rhine Falls to Record Low as Europe's Heatwave Cripples River Transport
excerpt: Water levels at the Rhine's Kaub chokepoint dropped to just 6 centimetres, well below the 2018 record, forcing most cargo transport onto trucks and trains.
body:
• The Rhine's water gauge at the Kaub chokepoint fell to 6 cm late Friday, smashing the previous 2018 record of 25 cm and effectively halting most commercial shipping.
  • German chemical producers, steelmakers, and utilities are reporting production disruptions, with Covestro declaring force majeure on polyether polyols.
  • Transport costs from Rotterdam to Karlsruhe have surged from €45 per ton in June to over €150, as freight shifts to road and rail.
  • The Kiel Institute estimates that 30 consecutive days with Kaub levels below 78 cm cuts German industrial production by 1%.

Water levels on the Rhine, one of Europe's most critical transport arteries, plunged to record lows on Saturday as an unrelenting heatwave continued to grip the continent. The crisis has forced most cargo transport off the river and onto trucks and trains, sending freight costs soaring and disrupting German industry.

Record-Shattering Lows

Data from Germany's inland navigation agency WSV showed the water level gauge at the Kaub chokepoint near Koblenz fell to just 6 centimetres late on Friday — less than a quarter of the previous record low of 25 cm set in 2018. By Saturday morning, the gauge had edged up marginally to 8 cm. The river is approximately one metre deeper than the gauge reading, but the numbers are so extreme that commercial shipping through Kaub has effectively ceased.

https://x.com/SPGEnergyOil/status/2088335861293219856

Kaub, located on a narrow stretch of the Rhine between Koblenz and Mainz, has been the river's most closely watched bottleneck for decades. Water levels there have been below the critical 78 cm threshold since mid-July, a sustained period that historically signals serious economic damage.

Industry Feels the Pain

German companies are reporting growing disruption. Chemicals giant Covestro declared force majeure on polyether polyols made at its Dormagen site, used in products like mattresses and refrigerator insulation, after the lack of transport capacity could not be fully offset by shifting volumes to trucks and trains.

"Alarm bells are ringing loudly: the extremely low water levels are increasingly pushing logistics and supply chains to their limits."

— Wolfgang Grosse Entrup, CEO, German Chemical Industry Association (VCI)

Chemical production at Evonik's Marl chemical park has been hampered by reduced cargoes. State-owned utility Uniper reported lower output at its German hydroelectric plants. Steel producer Salzgitter has been forced to transport coal by rail from Rotterdam to its HKM division in Duisburg, where logistics operator RheinCargo is now running three weekly freight train round trips to replace waterway deliveries.

Under normal conditions, HGK Dry Shipping moves around 24,000 metric tons of coal and ore per day from Rotterdam to Duisburg by river. That figure has dropped to approximately 14,500 tons, with the remainder now traveling by more expensive rail.

Costs Surge as Transport Shifts

The economic toll is mounting. The cost of tanker barge transport from Rotterdam to Karlsruhe has risen from roughly €45 per ton at the end of June to over €150, according to commodity traders. On northern sections of the river, where sailings continue, vessels are operating at just 20% capacity, requiring four to five times as many ships to move normal cargo volumes.

The Kiel Institute for the World Economy estimates that if the Kaub gauge stays below 78 cm for 30 straight days — as happened in 2022 and 2018 — German industrial production falls by approximately 1%. With levels already below that mark for a month, the drag on Europe's largest economy is becoming material.

What's Next

No significant rainfall is forecast in the Rhine catchment area in the near term, and meteorologists expect the heatwave to persist across much of Europe. Analysts warn that the crisis risks curbing German economic growth just as the country shows early signs of recovery. Local authorities in some regions have already relaxed weekend bans on truck driving to ease the pressure on road freight capacity. For an economy still dependent on its inland waterways for moving chemicals, fuels, ores, and agricultural products, the Rhine's record drought is an increasingly costly problem with no immediate solution.
